Name: continued_influence_belief
Title: Retracted but Not Erased: The Continued Influence of Corrected Misinformation in LLM Belief Representations
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM reads a false claim about an item that is later explicitly retracted in the same context, it verbally acknowledges the retraction yet retains an internally-decodable 'stale belief' in the retracted claim that continues to drive its downstream inferences — an LLM analogue of the human Continued Influence Effect (CIE). This internal residual belief is separable from the model's stated belief, predicts CIE-style reasoning errors, and can be causally erased by intervening on the component that carries it.
Related Work: The Continued Influence Effect / belief perseverance is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding: corrected misinformation continues to influence reasoning even after successful retraction (Chan et al. 2017 meta-analysis; Ecker et al. 2022 Nature Rev Psych; constraint-satisfaction models of perseverance, Read & Marcus-Newhall 2001; DIO model 2025). In LLMs, prior work studies (a) knowledge-editing reversibility and 'superficial editing' (Superficial Editing 2025; Believe It or Not 2025), (b) belief shifts under pretraining poisoning (Layer of Truth 2025), (c) intra-memory knowledge conflict localization (Where Knowledge Collides 2026), and (d) in-context knowledge conflict / sycophancy behaviorally. Crucially, to our knowledge no prior work isolate the CIE signature: a *within-context* retraction event after which the model behaviorally acknowledges the correction yet an internally-decodable belief in the *retracted* claim persists and continues to drive inferences. Prior belief-entrenchment work (Martingale Score; confirmation-bias CoT) concerns gradual non-Bayesian drift, not persistence of an explicitly-corrected proposition. We transfer a specific human-cognition phenomenon into LLMs, dissociate stated-vs-internal belief around a discrete correction, and give it a causal mechanistic treatment (locate + intervene), which is new. Delta to own-answer retraction work: here the false claim is EXTERNALLY supplied and explicitly retracted within the context, so any persistence cannot be explained by the model defending a claim it generated itself — a mechanistically distinct case that Experiment 3's own-answer-vs-external-claim contrast tests directly.
Abstract: People keep using misinformation even after they accept a correction — the Continued Influence Effect (CIE), one of the most robust findings in the misinformation literature. As LLMs increasingly ingest, then are corrected on, false claims within a single context (RAG updates, user retractions, multi-turn edits), we ask whether they inherit CIE at the level of their internal beliefs. We hypothesize that after an explicit in-context retraction of a false item-state claim, an LLM (i) verbally acknowledges the correction but (ii) retains a linearly-decodable residual belief in the retracted claim, (iii) this internal residual belief — not the stated belief — predicts continued reliance on the misinformation in downstream inference, and (iv) the residual can be causally erased by intervening on the component that carries it, reducing CIE-style errors. We build a controlled dataset of narratives/knowledge items in which a false claim is introduced and then retracted (with matched no-retraction and never-introduced controls), using both real-fact and synthetic-entity tracks to control priors, plus downstream inference probes whose correct answer depends on discarding the retracted claim. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read the internal belief in the retracted claim across layers, compute a per-item CIE residual (internal belief post-retraction minus never-introduced baseline), test whether it dissociates from stated belief and predicts downstream reliance (AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline), localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test a contrastive 'retraction-completion' steering intervention that drives the internal belief to baseline. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, CIE residual magnitude, stated-vs-internal dissociation, reliance-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention error reduction, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 scenarios built from scratch following the classic Continued-Influence paradigm, in two tracks: (a) ~2,500 real-fact narratives adapted from published CIE stimuli (a report asserts a cause, then retracts it); (b) ~2,500 synthetic-entity items ('Zorblax was reported to orbit Kelvath. Correction: this was an error.') with fully stipulated ground truth to remove pretraining priors. Each item appears in three conditions — RETRACTED, NO-RETRACTION, and NEVER-INTRODUCED (baseline) — with retraction strength varied (bare negation vs. explanatory alternative). Each item carries a stated-belief probe, a downstream open-inference probe whose correct answer requires discarding the retracted claim, and a comprehension check that a correction occurred. Items failing comprehension are dropped; ~4,000 remain. 80/20 item split; downstream open answers scored by an LLM-judge with human validation on a 300-item sample (target inter-rater κ ≥ 0.6).

Experiment 1 (H1 — after an accepted retraction the model keeps an internally-decodable residual belief in the retracted claim that is separable from its stated belief). Read the belief probe at the retracted-claim tokens WITHOUT asking the stated-belief question; CIE residual = belief(RETRACTED) − belief(NEVER-INTRODUCED) per item/layer. Systems compared: internal residual vs. the model's stated belief (which should read false) vs. the NO-RETRACTION condition. Decisive metric: mean CIE residual, and the per-item dissociation rate (stated=false while residual > 0). Convincing: residual ≥ 0.10 with CI excluding 0 in ≥ 3 of 4 models AND dissociation rate ≥ 30%, with explanatory-alternative retractions showing a smaller residual than bare negations (mirroring humans). Indecision band: residual < 0.05 or CI includes 0 → no continued influence internally (a valuable negative: LLMs fully erase corrected claims, unlike humans); 0.05–0.10 = suggestive only.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the internal residual predicts continued reliance on the misinformation beyond what the model says). Collect ground-truth downstream reliance from the open-inference probe. Decisive metric: AUROC of the residual predicting per-item reliance, compared against a log-prob-confidence baseline and against the stated-belief read-out. Convincing: residual AUROC ≥ 0.70 and at least +0.05 AUROC over both baselines (incremental signal). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or increment < 0.05 → residual not shown to add reliance-relevant information; ≤ 0.60 = negative.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the residual is carried by an identifiable component and can be causally erased). Localize via activation patching (RETRACTED↔NEVER-INTRODUCED) to the minimal head/layer set that removes the residual; derive a contrastive 'retraction-completion' steering direction. Decisive metric first: post-steering residual and downstream CIE-error rate; baselines: random-direction and truth-direction steering, plus the Setup guardrails. Convincing: subtraction drives residual to ≤ 0.05 and cuts CIE errors by ≥ 50% relative, cleanly on guardrails; adding the direction increases perseverance; random/truth directions cut errors < 10%. Indecision band: 20–50% error reduction or guardrails only in their 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no component/steer erases the residual without breaching guardrails) means CIE is distributed rather than a modular residual. Generalization (supports H1–H3): transfer across real and synthetic tracks and retraction phrasings, with transfer AUROC ≥ 0.70 and error-reduction retained ≥ 50%.

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The residual could reflect surface co-occurrence of the retracted claim's tokens rather than a genuine belief; matched NEVER-INTRODUCED controls, non-introduced distractors, comprehension checks, and paraphrase perturbations mitigate this. CIE may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs fully erase corrected claims — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans). Stated belief and downstream reliance may both fail simply because the model can't parse the retraction; comprehension checks and the RETRACTED-vs-NO-RETRACTION contrast disentangle parsing failure from perseverance. The residual may not be cleanly linear or single-locus; we report layerwise results and treat 'drive belief to baseline / reduce CIE' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Real-fact CIE stimuli may interact with pretraining priors; the synthetic track isolates the in-context mechanism. Downstream-reliance judgments require careful open-ended scoring (LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample). Steering could degrade fluency or over-suppress legitimately retained information; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.
